slides.about: Title, a Breaking Camp housekeeping slide for your announcements, one slide per lesson plus the two Trail Tools and the Financial Aid Trail Tip, this week's work, Mile Marker #5, and an in-class discussion. Every slide has a talk track in the speaker notes, so the deck also works as a script for an online mini-lecture.

coaching.head: Set the privacy ground rule early.
coaching.body: Money is personal, and some students are dealing with real hardship. Say it plainly in class and in your announcement: no assignment in this module asks for dollar amounts, and nobody is judged for their situation.

coaching.head: Question 2 is the hardest to write.
coaching.body: Students are asked to describe their financial situation honestly without numbers. Some write too little; a few overshare. Model the level of detail: "I work part-time and cover my own gas and phone; anything unexpected is hard" is enough.

coaching.head: Money leaks are the student's call.
coaching.body: Lesson 5.3 defines a leak as spending that doesn't match what the student values. Avoid feedback that judges choices (coffee, gaming, gifts). Ask whether it matches their priorities instead.

coaching.head: Question 5 rewards privacy habits.
coaching.body: The strongest answers say what the student left out of their AI prompts and how they described their situation in general terms. "I didn't use AI" is a complete answer.

coaching.head: Financial Aid questions will come to you.
coaching.body: The Trail Tip names two numbers that protect aid: a 2.0 GPA and a 67% completion rate. Students often don't know that a withdrawal counts against completion. Send schedule-change questions to Financial Aid before students act.

coaching.head: Money stress can be a warning sign.
coaching.body: If a student mentions they can't afford food, housing, or to stay enrolled, follow up privately and connect them with their Success Coach and the money help listed in Lesson 5.2.

coaching.head: The Inventory matters to the course.
coaching.body: The Appreciative Advising Inventory is completion only, but students' answers shape the course. Tell students what changed last time because of it; the Results in Action page in this guide has the details.

activities.title: Leak or priority?
activities.materials: A list of eight to ten everyday purchases on the screen
steps: Show purchases like a streaming service, a delivery fee, a gym membership, gas, a gift, and a late fee.
Students decide for each one, privately: leak or priority, for them?
Discuss: did everyone agree? Why not? Connect it to the lesson's definition of a leak.
activities.why: Shows that a leak depends on what each person values, and gives students language for Mile Marker #5, Question 1.
activities.online: Post the list as an anonymous poll and share the spread of answers in your next announcement.

activities.title: Give every dollar a job
activities.materials: A sample monthly income and expenses for a fictional student, plus the Budget Builder
steps: In pairs, students build a zero-based budget for the fictional student until every dollar has a job.
Introduce a surprise: a $150 car repair. What changes?
Debrief: what made the surprise easier or harder to absorb?
activities.why: Practices the Budget Builder with numbers that aren't anyone's own, so nobody has to share.
activities.online: Share the fictional student's numbers and the surprise expense, and suggest students try it before building their own.

activities.title: The two numbers
activities.materials: The Financial Aid Trail Tip on the screen
steps: Ask students to guess the two numbers that protect financial aid before showing them.
Reveal the 2.0 GPA and 67% completion rate, and explain how a withdrawal affects completion.
Ask: who would you contact before dropping a class?
activities.why: A quick, high-stakes fact many students learn too late.
activities.online: Put the two numbers in an announcement this week, with the Financial Aid contact.

discussion.title: The money tip you wish you'd known
prompt: What's one money tip you wish you'd learned sooner?
Did someone teach you, or did you learn it the hard way?
discussion.format: Talk with a partner for 3 minutes, then we'll build a class top-ten list.
discussion.source: An in-class version of the online discussion: What's One Money Tip You Really Wish You'd Learned Sooner?
discussion.facilitate: Set the ground rule first: no numbers, and tips are enough. If a student shares hardship, thank them, keep it moving, and follow up privately if needed.
